lines.text: infers that the whole idea of God is illusory. If he sees that
evil triumphs in the world and good succumbs, then he
doubts or despairs of God as being in sovereign control of
fate and history. When he sees the innumerable acts of folly
and madness in the world he begins to doubt the very idea
of God. How can God, if there is a God, allow this or that to
go on? Hence, he thinks, there is no God, there cannot be a God.
This is the characteristic judgment of modern man, voiced
again and again, and to-day especially many people are
speaking like this. There is no need for me to go into details.
In fact, both the parable of Jesus and ruthless fate give us the
same shock of offence repeatedly: it is not at all obvious to
man's perception that a God of justice and goodness reigns
supreme. The God of the parable is the sovereign Lord to
whose caprice man is surrendered, and in relation to whom
he has no rights or claims—and this too is the God who
does violence to man's conscience in the tragic mysteries of
human destiny. In both cases it is the same shock of offence!
The only difference is that the man of to-day draws the
conclusion that such a God is no God—whether he ends in
indifference and resignation, or whether he draws the further
conclusion that it is for human beings to take their lives in
this world into their own hands in disregard of God. Let us
make ourselves the masters, they say, we who are free and
steadfast in purpose! In any case, man does not really sur-
mount the obstacle implied in the offence that divine justice
is not perceptible, divine goodness is not demonstrable.
But is not this parable an offence for the Christian also
who wishes to submit himself humbly and sincerely to the
will of God? to the God whom the gospel proclaims to be the
God of grace? Is it the gospel which Jesus is preaching here?
Does not Jesus speak elsewhere of God as the heavenly
Father from whose providential goodness everyone may
draw consolation? Does He not speak of the God without
whose knowledge not a sparrow falls to the ground, who
feeds the ravens and clothes in beauty the flowers of the
field, and cares still more for us His children? God as the
